newsitem.title: INDIA: India denies provoking Pakistan ahead of talks.
newsitem.headline: India denies provoking Pakistan ahead of talks.

text.p: India on Thursday denied its military had provoked Pakistan ahead of planned talks between the arch-rivals and said New Delhi was committed to improving relations with its neighbours.
Pakistani Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan on Thursday accused India of increasing tension ahead of the high-level talks, tentatively set for next week in Islamabad.

At a news conference in Islamabad, Khan cited a recent alleged violation of Pakistani airspace, the reported deployment of medium-range ballistic missiles near the border and a border clash on Tuesday night.

A spokesman for the Indian Foreign Ministry restated New Delhi's denial that one of its jet fighters had flown over Pakistan earlier this month, breaking the sound barrier and rattling windows in Islamabad.
He also noted Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's statement on Wednesday denying that India had deployed ballistic missiles near to the border with Pakistan.
As for any border clash, the Foreign Ministry spokesman said that: "India has been subjected to unprovoked firing on several occasions across the border".
Indian and Pakistani troops often exchange small arms fire, and occasionally artillery shells, across the boundary dividing the Himalayan region of Kashmir between the long-time foes.
Pakistan's foreign minister said it was not clear whether the incidents he said had taken place had happened with Gujral's knowledge or were only the doing of the Indian armed forces.

"We would not like to muddy the waters by adopting strident positions," the Indian Foreign Ministry spokesman said, adding: "India's armed forces are not an independent source of power as they are subject to civilian authority."
The spokesman said India had given very clear, not mixed, signals ahead of the planned talks between the two nations' foreign secretaries -- the highest level career diplomats.
"Our position has been very clearly put across at the prime ministerial level," he said, referring to Gujral's meeting in the Maldives last month with his Pakistani counterpart, Nawaz Sharif.

The Foreign Ministry said Gujral's policy, which he first pursued as foreign minister before becoming prime minister in April, was to foster improved ties with South Asian neighbours. Gujral has said he is willing to offer concessions if need be.
"On account of this, there has been a visible change in the atmosphere on the subcontinent," the spokesman said.
"Our prime minister's initiative of reaching out to neighbours has been much appreciated," he said. "The signals from India have been very clear and very unambiguous."
